teaching.task: # HMS Year 11 V05 (Health for individuals and communities): the determinants of health. Why do some groups of Australians end up with worse health, and why can't "they should choose better" explain it? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: The things that shape health are called determinants, and the syllabus sorts them into five groups. They act in order, from society down to the body. Broad features of society come first, like culture, education systems, jobs and the media. Then environmental factors, like housing, transport and safe places to walk. Then socioeconomic characteristics, like income, education and occupation. Then health behaviours, like diet, exercise and smoking. And last, biomedical factors, like blood pressure and weight. A clinic treats the bottom of the stack. But the top is what moves a whole population. These groups don't act one at a time. They interact, in three ways. The first is a chain, where one determinant produces the next. Take a rural community. Specialist services and jobs are concentrated in the cities. That puts care a long way away. Distance makes seeing a specialist cost a day's pay and petrol, so people put it off. And when they finally go, the condition is further along. Every link is ordinary. The chain is what does the damage. The second way is clustering. Disadvantages tend to arrive together, low income with insecure housing, risky work and poor transport. Because they cluster, their effects compound, so together they do more harm than each would alone. The third way is feedback. Illness makes it harder to work, which cuts income, which worsens the conditions that caused the illness. Put all this together across Australia, and you get the social gradient. Health improves at every step up the income ladder, not just at the bottom. So this isn't only about poverty. It's about how resources are spread across everyone.

- **Added beyond the site.** (a) A live two-group campaign model (scene 8, illustrative). (b) The social gradient as a coded staircase (illustrative). (c) Attempt 1 is the site's Activity 2 as a short exam item.
- **Entry knowledge.** hms-y11-m1-v02 (circumstances change health directly and change the range of choices); hms-y11-m1-v04 (equity, access, the inequity test); hms-y11-m1-v03 (averages hide groups). - **Terms.** Determinant (2, "anything that influences health, for a person or a whole population"); each group by its examples (2); upstream and downstream (2, "the social conditions that shape health" and "the body-level factors closest to the outcome"); social gradient (4, "health improves at every step up"); sociological (5, "about people's situations, not their character"); norm (5, "what's usual in a person's setting").

Interaction kinds draw on it as coloured paths (chain: one path down; clustering: several boxes lighting together with a compounding readout; feedback: an arrow running back up). The **campaign model** is a coded two-group readout board. People are never drawn; babies, families and groups are objects, places, coded blocks and labels.
- **Attempt.** 10a (Revision 2): the site's Activity 2 idea on an unseen case: "A national campaign gives every young person a free fitness app with home workout plans. Explain how this campaign could improve the national average while widening the gap between groups." (3 marks). 10c: WE b1 verbatim: "Explain how determinants of health interact to affect the health of a population group." (5 marks).
- **Memory aids.** The site's two book lines: "Upstream shapes, downstream gets treated" (from the stack's two arrows) and "An intervention that requires resources to act on will help most those who have the most resources" (shortened for speech). Scene 9, after scenes 2 and 8.
- **A mistake/fix scene** is not included. "Behaviours are furthest upstream" is answered in scene 2; "only the poorest have worse health" in scene 4; "they should choose better" in scenes 5 and 6; "a list of five determinants" is crossed in 10d; "the campaign worked, so the gap closed" in 10b.
- **Reuse:** explainer kit, shared scenes; v04's `AccessGates` strip (scene 1, 2); v01 and v02 plates `hms-insecure-housing-v1.png` (scene 3), `hms-shift-roster-apron-v1.png` (scene 4); v04's `hms-regional-clinic-v1.png` (scene 3, small); Module 6 b01 parts, `WrongChip`. New in `hms-shared`: `DeterminantsChain`, `GradientSteps`, `CampaignModel`.
- **Colour key.** The five groups, top to bottom: broad features of society violet; environmental olive; socioeconomic amber; health behaviours teal; biomedical blue. Advantaged group cool; disadvantaged group warm. Interaction paths ink with arrowheads in the colour of the box they reach. Answers green; crossed mistakes red only.
- **Type sizes.** As the course brief.
- **Anchor.** The `DeterminantsChain` is the anchor, solid from scene 2 (about 820 px tall at the left), present in scenes 3 to 7 and in feedback 10d. Painted plates attach to its boxes: new `hms-suburb-takeaway-strip-v1.png` (twelve takeaway shopfronts and no greengrocer) for the environment and behaviour link, new `hms-remote-road-sign-v1.png` (a long outback road with a blank distance sign) for the rural chain, and reused plates above.
- **Simulation.** Scene 8's `CampaignModel` (illustrative, labelled): two equal-sized groups with a health index, advantaged 80 and disadvantaged 60 (average 70, gap 20). The campaign offers the same possible gain of 10 points to each, but the share of people with the resources to act on it is 60 per cent in the advantaged group and 20 per cent in the disadvantaged group. Gains 6 and 2; new values 86 and 62; average 74 (up 4), gap 24 (up 4). Readouts "average" and "gap" read from the model. - **Board stages.** (1) the v04 gates with empty boxes, then the bracelets, scene 1; (2) the determinants chain, scenes 2 to 4 (the chain carries interactions as overlays); (3) the gradient staircase, scene 4 end; (4) the causes board, scenes 5 and 6; (5) the groups board, scene 7; (6) the campaign model, scene 8; (7) memory, questions, handoff and notes. Longest set-up: the chain, scenes 2 to 4 (about 1,450 characters, about 110 s), kept alive by three different interaction overlays, two plates and a readout.
- **Open decisions for root.** (1) Three new plates. (2) The dated AIHW figure is in (root ruling); it carries a release re-check flag.

Main question: *Why do some groups of Australians end up with worse health, and why can't "they should choose better" explain it?*

Handoff: the same chain, pointed at young people (route entry hms-y11-m1-v06). **Handoff frame (v06 opens from it):** the determinants chain at the left of centre (about 75 per cent of frame height), all five boxes labelled and in their colours; an amber tag "young people" sits on top of the stack with a short arrow into the first box; the "Next" chip at the lower right reads "Next: are young people today really so different?"; this video's heading at the top left.

15 voiced scene files (1 to 9, 10a to 10d, 11, 12). No people appear at any point.

scenes.teachingReason: The things that shape health are called determinants, and the syllabus sorts them into five groups. They act in order, from society down to the body. Broad features of society come first, like culture, education systems, jobs and the media. Then environmental factors, like housing, transport and safe places to walk. Then socioeconomic characteristics, like income, education and occupation. Then health behaviours, like diet, exercise and smoking. And last, biomedical factors, like blood pressure and weight. A clinic treats the bottom of the stack. But the top is what moves a whole population.

scenes.teachingReason: The second way is clustering. Disadvantages tend to arrive together, low income with insecure housing, risky work and poor transport. Because they cluster, their effects compound, so together they do more harm than each would alone. The third way is feedback. Illness makes it harder to work, which cuts income, which worsens the conditions that caused the illness. Put all this together across Australia, and you get the social gradient. Health improves at every step up the income ladder, not just at the bottom. So this isn't only about poverty. It's about how resources are spread across everyone.

Control: prevention is an investment in a future you have to believe in. And belonging: some behaviours are part of fitting in.
